body:
Yes, `codespell` doesn't like Jolt's `JPH::StreamIn` type, found in `jolt_stream_wrappers.h`, because it thinks it's a misspelling of "streaming".

I tried doing a line ignore with `// codespell:ignore StreamIn`, but that just caused more warnings about the same "misspelling" within the ignore comment itself, for some strange reason.

I saw some other PRs had just tacked on to this global exclusion list instead, so I went ahead and did the same. I figured someone would let me know if there's a better way.

body: It's a Jolt feature. An elastic collision is a collision with restitution != 0, basically it determines the velocity that is needed before the restitution calculations will kick in. If the velocity is lower than this value, the simulation will treat the collision as having restitution = 0 regardless of what the user specified.

If I understand this right:
```suggestion
			Which of the two nodes bound by a joint should represent the world when one of the two is omitted, as either [member Joint3D.node_a] or [member Joint3D.node_b]. This can be thought of as having the omitted node be a [StaticBody3D] at the joint's position.
```

body:
Maybe it sounds silly, but seeing as how Godot refers to restitution as bounce in its physics materials (hence the setting name), would it be wrong to just say this instead?

```suggestion
			The minimum velocity needed before a collision can be bouncy, in meters per second.
```

Seems fine, but I'm curious on what was the issue there caused specifically by adding Jolt?

body:
Should we really enable Jolt asserts on dev builds? I understand the rationale that in a dev build we might want all debug features enabled, but in practice the vast majority of users of dev builds won't be Jolt experts and won't have much use for it crashing on them.

For this kind of stuff, in my experience it's used occasionally on demand by the feature's maintainer to debug specific issues, in which case it could be made a module-specific SCons argument (see `modules/minimp3/config.py` for an example of that).

I'm not too strongly opinionated about it though, and we can start with it enabled in all dev builds and see if it turns out to be a bother for engine contributors.

A subsidiary question is: aside from ObjectStream, do we compile/use all files from Jolt? If not, would it make sense to remove more of them, or would that be too much hassle?

The linker can be somewhat trusted to drop unused code so it shouldn't affect binary size, but compiling everything does affect compile time, and including all files (including their diffs on subsequent updates) impacts repo size.

Not a blocker for this PR in any case.

body:
The assert is implemented in `jolt_globals.cpp` as an `ERR_PRINT`, as seen [here](https://github.com/mihe/godot/blob/828ab604c101616f1a2f27f85a1af39f0021cf8b/modules/jolt_physics/jolt_globals.cpp#L78-L81), so it doesn't crash anything per se.

I guess the point still stands that most people won't know what to do about the error once they do see it printed, but I've found that it's easy to think that everything is fine only to fire up a dev build and see Jolt trigger a bunch of asserts because something somewhere is ill-formed, so my vote would probably be to leave this enabled until it's found to be too annoying.

`memnew` (and `memnew_allocator`) in particular wasn't a problem for Jolt, but `memnew_placement` was, as placement new will try to use the class-defined `new` operators, which Jolt implements for most of its classes (through its [`JPH_OVERRIDE_NEW_DELETE`](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/c10d9b2a8ee134fb5e72de1a0f26f8c9cc8f6382/Jolt/Core/Memory.h#L30-L39) macro) in order to use its allocator hooks.

This meant you couldn't put Jolt stuff in containers like `HashSet` or `LocalVector`, as they use `memnew_placement`, which led to compilation errors about signature mismatches with the class-specific `new` operators that Jolt defines, which adding a global qualifier to the placement new resolves, as it stops the compiler from trying to use these class-specific operators.

I thought it looked odd for only `memnew_placement` to have the global qualifier, so I threw it in for `memnew` and `memnew_allocator` as well, since I figured the intention was always for those to invoke the global operators declared in `memory.h` anyway.

However, I just now found that you can actually define a placement new on a per-class basis as well, which I had no idea about, by simply doing this:

```cpp
void *operator new (size_t size, void *ptr) noexcept { return ptr; }
```

... which I must admit looks a bit strange, but adding that to Jolt's `JPH_OVERRIDE_NEW_DELETE` macro does seem to resolve the compilation error as well, without needing to touch `memory.h`.

Do you see any problems with adding that on your end, @jrouwe?

(There's probably some discussion to be had regarding Godot's containers not respecting the alignment of its contained items as well, which I imagine makes them ill-suited for storing a lot of Jolt's types in the first place, since a lot of them are 16-byte aligned or more due to its use of SIMD.)

Thanks for the detailed explanation!

It seems fine to me to change `memory.h` to add `::` for disambiguation.

Whether Jolt would benefit from also defining placement new operators to avoid such issues in the future, I'll leave to Jorrit to decide, but this shouldn't block this PR either way.
